issue.issue_text: Whether the benefit of acquittal granted to the appellant should also be extended to a co-accused who has not filed an appeal.

facts: An appellant and a co-accused (Sk. Sahid @ Bablu) were both convicted of murder by the lower courts.
Only the appellant challenged the conviction by filing an appeal to the Supreme Court; the co-accused did not.
The advocate for the State (the respondent) conceded that if the appellant were acquitted, the benefit of that acquittal should also be extended to the non-appealing co-accused.
law: The Court relied on its own precedent, specifically the case of *Bijoy Singh v. State of Bihar*.

The legal principle established in that case is that if, upon evaluation of the evidence, the court concludes that a conviction of *any* accused was not possible, the benefit of an acquittal must be extended to a similarly situated co-accused, even if that co-accused has not filed an appeal.
application: The Court evaluated the prosecution's case and found that the evidence against both the appellant and the non-appealing co-accused was insufficient for a conviction. The case rested on weak identification evidence which the court found could not form the basis for a guilty verdict.
Since the court concluded that "no conviction of any accused was possible" based on the evidence presented, it determined that the legal principle from the *Bijoy Singh* case was directly applicable.
The non-appealing co-accused was deemed to be "similarly situated" to the appellant, as the case against both of them failed for the same reasons.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided to extend the benefit of the acquittal to the non-appealing co-accused. It did so by applying the established legal principle that when the evidence is found to be insufficient to convict any of the accused, the acquittal must also be granted to a co-accused who is in the same position, even if they did not appeal their conviction.
